passage:
For years I took the rail for granted,
a grey bar bolted to grey planks,
and if I thought of it at all
I thought: someone has let this go.

The varnish had quit in the middle third.
Bare wood showed through like a scar
where the finish had been rubbed away,
and I called that damage, walking past.

This morning the fog came in early
and the six-ten was late, so I stood
with nothing to do but look down
at the place where the varnish had failed.

It was not a scar. It was a shine.
The wood there was darker and smoother
than anywhere else along the rail,
polished the way a doorstep is polished.

I put my hand where the shine was.
It fit. Of course it fit. It was made
of the fitting, of ten thousand palms
arriving at the same stretch of pine,

because that is where the gangway tilts
and everyone reaches at the same step.
The rail had not been neglected.
The rail had been used, and had answered,

giving up its hard coat at the one place
it was asked for, and giving up nothing
at the ends, where no one needs it,
where the varnish is perfect and dead.

I have been wrong about wear.
I had thought it the opposite of care,
the slow proof that no one was minding.
Now I think a surface can be a ledger

kept in the plainest hand there is:
here is where we held on, and here,
and here. The horn came through the fog.
I let go of the rail and went down.

correct_answer: a speaker who comes to see a record of long use in an object she had passed for years
explanation: The closing movement states the revision directly: "I have been wrong about wear... Now I think a surface can be a ledger / kept in the plainest hand there is: / here is where we held on." The worn stretch is read as a record of the many hands that used it.

Everyone has a plan for the kitchen.
Raise the floor eight inches, says Ruth.
Tile, not board, says her husband,
and put the outlets up at chest height.

They are not wrong. The river will come
again, in seven years or eleven,
and the outlets at ankle height
are the reason we have no stove.

But I notice they begin at the rebuild.
They arrive at the door with a plan
the way you bring a casserole:
something warm to set down and leave.

What I want is slower than tile.
I want someone to stand in the doorway
and let me say what was in the room.
The table my father cut down

to fit the corner when we moved,
which was too short for six, and we used it
for twenty years for six.
The tin of buttons. The step stool

with my brother's name in nail polish.
Say them back to me. Do not tell me
buttons can be replaced, which is true,
which is the least useful true thing.

Ruth, I will raise the floor.
I will put the outlets where you say.
But not this week. This week
the room is still a room to me

and not a site. So stand here.
Look where the water stopped
on the door frame, that grey line,
and say: it came this high, and this

is what it took. Then we can measure.
Then bring me the tile.

The Ashcombe Museum has spent two years rehanging its natural history floor, and the whole redesign follows from one decision: the cases are now grouped by habitat instead of by period. Everything the new floor does well, and the one thing it cannot do at all, comes out of that single choice.

The gain arrives immediately. In the first room a river is assembled entire — otter, kingfisher, caddis larva, and the silt all three depend on — and a child can see in ten seconds why the heron stands where it stands. The old chronological hang put the kingfisher three rooms away from the fish it eats, and visitors under twelve almost never made the connection. Grouping by habitat makes relationships visible, and relationships are what a child comes for.

Follow the decision further and it begins to charge for itself. Because a habitat is a snapshot, these rooms cannot easily show change. The marsh room holds specimens gathered across ninety years without saying so; a curlew shot in 1908 stands beside one found dead in 1994, and the label gives neither date. A visitor who wants to know whether there are fewer curlews now has to go and ask at the desk.

By the last gallery the bill is paid in full. The final room is titled "The Changing Coast," and it is the one room that needs the arrangement the museum has given up: it wants a sequence, and the floor no longer supplies one. The curators have improvised with a wall of dated photographs, which works, though it works the way a poster works and not the way the rest of the floor works. You read it standing still, instead of walking through it.

None of this is an argument for putting the clocks back. The river room is the best thing the Ashcombe has done in a decade, and no chronological hang could have produced it. It is an argument for admitting that one room was left carrying a whole dimension the rehang surrendered, and that a wall of captions is not stout enough to carry it.

Ask why the tomato took so long to reach the British table and you will be told that people thought it poisonous. The story is on museum labels and in the front matter of cookbooks: the tomato belongs to the nightshade family, so for two centuries Britons grew it for ornament and would not eat it.

The explanation should be dropped altogether. The trouble is not that the evidence for it is thin; the trouble is that the evidence runs the other way. English herbals describe the plant from the 1590s, and those that mention eating it mention it calmly, as something done in Spain and Italy rather than as something fatal. Gardening manuals of the 1700s give instructions for raising the fruit for the kitchen. If a fear had been general, these writers are exactly the people who would have recorded it, and they did not.

What did hold the tomato back is duller and far better attested: the plant would not ripen. A tomato needs a long warm season, and the English summer supplies neither reliably. Growers got green fruit in most years, and green fruit, in a kitchen with no tradition of cooking it down, is simply not food. The nightshade story explains a refusal. There was no refusal to explain — only a crop that failed.

The dates settle the matter. Tomatoes entered ordinary British cookery not when a superstition lifted but when glass became cheap. Sheet glass and hot-water piping made the commercial glasshouse practical in the 1830s and 1840s, and tomato recipes appear in ordinary household books within that same generation: not a decade after any change in belief, but a decade after a change in horticulture.

The poison story survives because it is a better anecdote than a greenhouse. It supplies the past with a vivid error to be rescued from, which flatters the present, and it can be repeated without reading anything. The truer account asks for a little more: a seed catalogue, a weather record, and the price of glass.
